title: Cassini, 1997 — the probe that found an ocean, then dived into Saturn to protect it
sources: Wikipedia: Cassini–Huygens — launched on a Titan IVB/Centaur on 15 October 1997 from Cape Canaveral; nearly 20 years in space, almost 7 in transit, 13 orbiting Saturn (orbit from 1 July 2004); powered by plutonium RTGs because, at Saturn's distance from the Sun, solar arrays were not feasible; Huygens entered Titan's atmosphere on 14 January 2005 and landed; Cassini observed water-ice geysers at the south pole of Enceladus; in 2014 NASA reported evidence of a large salty internal ocean there, 'among the most likely places in the Solar System to host alien microbial life'; on 15 September 2017 it was sent into Saturn's atmosphere and burned up, to prevent contaminating moons that might offer habitable environments to stowaway terrestrial microbes, once it could no longer be manoeuvred; it burned up about 45 seconds after its last transmission
Wikipedia: Huygens (spacecraft) — the first spacecraft to land on Titan and the farthest landing from Earth a spacecraft has ever made
Wikipedia: The Day the Earth Smiled — composite photograph taken by Cassini on 19 July 2013; Carolyn Porco's idea that people look up and smile; NASA's related 'Wave at Saturn' event
Also on this day (candidates.md, in the app): 1815 Napoleon begins his exile on Saint Helena; 1888 the 'From Hell' letter, allegedly from Jack the Ripper, is received
Film (public domain, NASA): 'Kennedy Marks 20th Anniversary of Cassini Arrival' (1997 footage: assembly, RTGs, the launch); NASA/JPL animation 'Cassini's Grand Finale' (2017)
Pictures (public domain, NASA/JPL): Titan IVB on Launch Complex 40; Saturn from Cassini, 2004; Saturn's rings, 2013; Enceladus; The Day the Earth Smiled, 2013; A Farewell to Saturn, 2017
Illustrative stock footage (Pexels, free licence; not of the event): a night sky

post.facebook:
On this day in 1997, the Cassini spacecraft launched from Cape Canaveral on a Titan IV rocket, bound for Saturn.

So far from the Sun that solar panels would not work, it ran on plutonium. It reached Saturn seven years later, and dropped the Huygens probe onto the moon Titan — still the farthest landing ever made from Earth. Then, at a tiny moon called Enceladus, it found geysers of ice — and evidence of a salty ocean beneath, one of the likeliest places in the Solar System to host alien life.

In 2013 Cassini turned to photograph Earth, and people were asked to look up and smile. We were a single dot of light under Saturn's rings.

When it could soon no longer be steered, NASA chose not to risk a crash that might carry Earth microbes to those moons. On 15 September 2017, Cassini dived into Saturn, on purpose, and burned up about 45 seconds after its last signal.

Also on 15 October: Napoleon's exile on Saint Helena began (1815), and the "From Hell" letter was received (1888).

youtube.description:
Cassini launched on 15 October 1997. Powered by plutonium, it reached Saturn seven years later, landed the Huygens probe on Titan — the farthest landing ever made — and found ice geysers and a hidden salty ocean on the moon Enceladus, one of the likeliest places to find alien life. In 2013 it photographed Earth as a single dot of light. Then, before it could no longer be steered, it was sent into Saturn on purpose so it could never contaminate those moons — burning up about 45 seconds after its last signal.

Also on 15 October: Napoleon's exile on Saint Helena (1815) and the "From Hell" letter (1888).
